title: Local and Global Extrema
quickIdea: A local maximum beats its own neighbourhood; a global maximum beats the whole domain. The same point can be one, both, or neither.
remember: f has a local (relative) maximum at c if f(c) >= f(x) for every x in some open interval around c; local minimum is the same with <=.
f has a global (absolute) maximum at c if f(c) >= f(x) for every x in the whole domain under discussion; global minimum likewise.
Local compares against nearby points only; global compares against every point of the domain. A global extremum that is interior is also local; a local one need not be global.
Extremum is the collective word for a maximum or a minimum point; the extremal value is f at that point.

Whether an endpoint can be a local extremum is a definitional choice, not a theorem: many textbooks restrict local extrema to interior points, and GATE has used the wider convention (see the endpoint card).

example.prompt: For f(x) = x^2 on the domain [-1, 2], name every local extremum and every global extremum.
example.work: f'(x) = 2x vanishes only at x = 0. On (-1, 1) the value 0 is the smallest nearby value, so x = 0 is a local minimum, and f(0) = 0 is also the smallest value on the whole domain, so it is the global minimum too. At the right endpoint f(2) = 4, which is larger than every nearby value inside the domain, but it is not a local maximum under the interior convention because no two-sided neighbourhood of 2 lies in the domain.
example.answer: Local minimum at 0 (value 0), which is also the global minimum. Global maximum 4 at x = 2, which is an endpoint and therefore not a local maximum in the interior sense.

gateAngle: GATE states extrema questions on a closed interval more often than on the whole line, and the closed interval is exactly where the local/global distinction bites. GATE CSE 1997 Q.4.1 asks for the maximum on [0,2] and the answer is at the endpoint; GATE CSE 2012 Q.9 asks for the number of local minima and the answer depends on whether the left endpoint counts.

variations.label: ORIGINAL PYQ-STYLE QUESTION
variations.question: For f(x) = x^3 - x on [-1, 1], how many local maxima and how many local minima are there inside the open interval?
variations.answer: One of each: a local maximum at x = -1/sqrt(3) with value 2/(3 sqrt(3)) and a local minimum at x = 1/sqrt(3) with value -2/(3 sqrt(3)).
variations.why: Same recipe on a cubic whose critical points are irrational. The step that changes is only the arithmetic of f at the critical points.

variations.label: CONCEPTUAL PRACTICE QUESTION
variations.question: Can a point be a global maximum but not a local maximum?
variations.answer: Yes, when the domain has an endpoint that is the highest point: f(x) = x on [0,1] has its global maximum at x = 1 and x = 1 has no two-sided neighbourhood inside the domain, so it is not a local maximum under the interior convention.
variations.why: It separates the two definitions from the single word 'maximum'. GATE CSE 2012 Q.9 is decided by exactly this point.

trap.what: Treating 'local maximum' and 'global maximum' as the same thing, or assuming the highest point of a closed interval must be a stationary point.
trap.why: On a closed interval the largest value is often at an endpoint, where the derivative is one-sided and need not vanish; and a local maximum can be lower than a global maximum elsewhere.
trap.counterexample: f(x) = x^2 on [-1, 2] has its global maximum 4 at the endpoint 2, where f'(2) = 4 is not zero, while the only stationary point gives the minimum.

check.question: f(x) = x^3 - 3x on [-2, 2]. What is the global minimum and where is it attained?
check.answer: The global minimum is -2, attained at both x = -1 and x = -2.
check.explanation: f(-2) = -2, f(-1) = 2, f(1) = -2, f(2) = 2. Two points give -2: the critical point x = -1 and the left endpoint x = -2. A global minimum may be attained at more than one point.
